meta.blurb: Ines repairs bicycles all day and still feels she is rushing, never steering. On her wall hangs her grandfather's brass compass. Then a big chain shop opens nearby and makes her an offer, and she must decide what she stands for.
meta.bible: Ines: the owner of Second Wheel, a small bike repair shop; practical, hard-working and tired at the start; the book follows her for about one year. Second Wheel: the shop, with a workbench at the back and a brass compass on the wall. The compass: belonged to Ines's grandfather, a ship's mechanic; it points to magnetic north and can be thrown off by iron or magnets nearby. Karim: her young helper, learning to be a mechanic. Mr Weiss: an older customer whose late wife's bicycle needs repair. Lucia: Ines's sister. Velo World: a large chain shop that opens nearby. The Sunday review: Ines's weekly twenty minutes of planning. Ines's five values: honesty, craft, family, learning, kindness. Four areas to look after: body, mind, people, purpose. Voice and tone: calm, concrete and encouraging; a principle is a direction, not a rule; one clear idea in every beat; no studies or numbers are invented.

beats.scene: Ines works at a crowded bench in her bike repair shop
beats.summary: Ines is always busy in her bike shop but feels she is reacting rather than steering.

beats.scene: An old brass compass hangs on the wall above the workbench
beats.summary: Her grandfather's compass shows direction, not speed.

beats.scene: Ines sits alone at the counter with a cup of tea and a notepad
beats.summary: Being busy is not the same as going somewhere that matters.

beats.scene: Ines writes a long list of words on a page beside the compass
beats.summary: Values are the things you would keep even if nobody ever saw you choose them.

beats.scene: Ines crosses words out one by one until only a few remain
beats.summary: Cutting the list to five forces honest choices.

beats.scene: Five words are written in large letters on a card pinned near the compass
beats.summary: Ines's five values are honesty, craft, family, learning and kindness.

beats.scene: Ines sketches a flag on a hill and an arrow off the page
beats.summary: A goal is a place to reach, while a value is a direction that never runs out.

beats.scene: Ines remembers her grandfather repairing an engine in a small workshop
beats.summary: Many values come from family and experience, and you can choose to keep them.

beats.scene: A red-faced customer shouts across the counter while Ines holds a wheel
beats.summary: Between what happens and what we do there is a gap, and in it we choose.

beats.scene: Ines writes two sentences on a whiteboard, one crossed out
beats.summary: Changing the words from I have to into I choose to makes us feel more in control.

beats.scene: Two circles on a notepad, a large one with a small one inside
beats.summary: Some things we can control and some we cannot, and energy is best spent on the first.

beats.scene: Through the shop window Ines sees a large new shop with a bright sign
beats.summary: A large chain shop called Velo World opens nearby, and Ines worries.

beats.scene: Ines writes a list of things she can do on a small card
beats.summary: Ines decides to compete honestly, without saying anything untrue about her rival.

beats.scene: Ines holds a worn part at the workbench while a customer waits outside
beats.summary: A part is worn but still works, and the customer would not notice if she sold a new one.

beats.scene: Ines talks gently to a customer and shows him the unworn part
beats.summary: Ines tells the customer the truth, and loses a little money now but gains his trust.

beats.scene: Ines hangs her apron on a hook and looks at her tidy workbench
beats.summary: Integrity means that what you say and what you do match, and it builds self-trust.

beats.scene: Ines ties her running shoes by the shop door in the grey early light
beats.summary: Keeping small promises to yourself builds self-respect.

beats.scene: Ines places a new notebook beside the kettle where she makes her morning tea
beats.summary: New habits stick when they are tiny and linked to something you already do.

beats.scene: Ines writes a letter at her desk with the compass behind her
beats.summary: Ines writes a letter from her future self describing a good ordinary year.

beats.scene: Karim sweeps the floor of the shop while Ines watches him thoughtfully
beats.summary: Ines sets a yearly goal that follows her values: to train Karim as a full mechanic.

beats.scene: Ines draws a ladder of small steps on a large sheet of paper
beats.summary: A big goal is broken into weekly steps.

beats.scene: Her phone buzzes with messages while a half-built wheel waits on the bench
beats.summary: Some tasks shout for attention and some matter more, and they are not always the same.

beats.scene: A small sign on the door of the shop says Back at noon
beats.summary: Ines protects a quiet morning each Friday for planning and teaching.

beats.scene: Ines sits with a mug and a notebook on a quiet Sunday afternoon
beats.summary: A twenty-minute weekly review keeps her days aligned with her values.

beats.scene: Ines shakes her head politely at a man holding out an old bicycle
beats.summary: Saying no to some requests protects the things she has said yes to.

beats.scene: A weekly calendar fills with coloured blocks around a clock
beats.summary: Everyone has the same 168 hours in a week, and choices decide how they are spent.

beats.scene: Ines sleeps soundly in a small bed with the window open to the night
beats.summary: Rest is part of the plan, because a tired person chooses worse.

beats.scene: Ines writes prices on a small chalkboard outside the shop
beats.summary: Fair prices are a way of living by her values, and she explains them openly.

beats.scene: Karim stands with a bent wheel in his hands and a worried face
beats.summary: Karim breaks a customer's wheel, and Ines treats the mistake as a lesson.

beats.scene: Ines and Karim stand side by side at the workbench with a new wheel
beats.summary: Ines keeps Karim accountable and fair: they fix the problem and pay for the wheel together.

beats.scene: Ines listens carefully to an older man and examines his bicycle
beats.summary: Like a good mechanic, Ines asks questions to understand a problem before she tries to fix it.

beats.scene: Mr Weiss strokes the old frame of a bicycle with a sad expression
beats.summary: Mr Weiss is angry at a repair bill, but his real concern is his late wife's bicycle.

beats.scene: Ines and Mr Weiss shake hands over a handwritten agreement
beats.summary: Ines looks for a fair agreement in which both sides gain, and finds one with Mr Weiss.

beats.scene: Ines declines a very large order from a buyer with a firm handshake
beats.summary: When no fair deal exists, an honest no deal is better than a bad one.

beats.scene: Ines and Karim work together at the front counter and the workbench
beats.summary: Strengths differ, and combining them makes the shop better.

beats.scene: A small team sits on stools around the workbench for a short meeting
beats.summary: Weekly meetings and shared values help the team agree without constant orders.

beats.scene: Ines speaks seriously with Karim over a half-finished brake repair
beats.summary: When honesty and kindness pull apart, Ines finds a way to be both.

beats.scene: Ines and Lucia sit together at the kitchen table, talking quietly
beats.summary: Ines talks honestly with Lucia and they agree on a smaller loan and a clear plan.

beats.scene: A smartly dressed manager from Velo World holds out an offer in the shop
beats.summary: Velo World offers to buy Second Wheel for good money.

beats.summary: Ines tests the offer against her five values, and the answer is not simple.

beats.scene: Ines hands back a folder and shakes the manager's hand politely
beats.summary: Ines declines the offer for her own reasons, without judging people who would accept.

beats.scene: Ines bangs a tool on the bench in front of a rude customer
beats.summary: In a bad month Ines falls short of her values and loses her temper.

beats.scene: Ines holds the compass in her hand and tilts it near a metal toolbox
beats.summary: A compass can be thrown off by iron nearby, and people drift too, so they must correct course.

beats.summary: She joins a monthly repair day at the community hall and teaches children to fix bikes.

beats.scene: A simple drawing shows four circles labelled with body, mind, people and purpose
beats.summary: Ines looks after four areas of life: body, mind, people and purpose.

beats.scene: Ines studies a manual for electric bicycles at a lamp-lit table
beats.summary: Ines keeps learning by studying how to repair electric bicycles.

beats.scene: Ines reads her old letter at the counter on a cold March morning
beats.summary: A year later Ines rereads her letter and sees how far she has come.

beats.scene: Karim holds up a finished wheel while Ines nods proudly beside him
beats.summary: Karim becomes a full mechanic, and Ines passes the compass idea on to him.

beats.scene: Ines locks the shop door at sunset with the compass glowing on the wall
beats.summary: Principles are a direction to choose, check and correct, not a set of rules.

B1B2: Ines is busy from morning until night in her small bike shop. She fixes everything that comes in, but she has no idea where her days are leading.
A brass compass that belonged to her grandfather hangs above the workbench. One quiet evening Ines notices that it tells you which way to go, not how fast.
Ines understands that being busy is not the same as moving forward. She sits down with a notepad and asks herself what really matters to her.
Ines writes a list of twenty words, such as honesty, comfort, success and family. A value, she decides, is something you would choose even if nobody ever saw you do it.
Cutting the list down is painful, because every word seems good. Ines is forced to decide which ones she would protect first when life gets hard.
Ines writes her five words on a card and pins it beside the compass. They are honesty, craft, family, learning and kindness, and now she can see them every day.
Ines learns that a goal is a place you can reach and tick off. A value is more like north, because you can travel toward it for ever and never arrive.
Ines wonders where her values came from, and she sees her grandfather in every one. Some values are inherited, but you can choose to keep them as your own.
A customer shouts about a late repair, and Ines feels her anger rise. She remembers that between an event and her reaction there is a small gap, and she can choose in it.
Ines begins to notice how often she says that she has to do things. She tries saying that she chooses to, and her days feel lighter.
Ines cannot control the weather, the price of parts or what customers say online. She can control her own work, her words and her next small step.
A big chain called Velo World opens a shop two streets away. Ines worries that her customers will leave and her shop will not survive.
Ines decides that she will compete by doing excellent work and not by criticising her rival. If she does not tell the truth, she thinks, there is no point in winning.
A customer asks Ines to fix his brakes, but the old part is still good. He would never know if she sold him a new one.
Ines tells the customer that his brakes do not need changing yet. She loses a small sale, but he thanks her, and he returns the next month with two friends.
Ines notices that she feels lighter when her actions match her words. A person who keeps breaking small promises, she thinks, slowly stops trusting herself.
Ines promises herself a short walk before work each morning. Keeping such a small promise, day after day, makes her trust herself more.
Ines wants to write one line in a notebook each day, so she puts it next to the kettle. Linking a new habit to an old one makes it much easier.
Ines writes a letter as if she were five years older, describing an ordinary good day. Seeing her future so clearly helps her see what to do now.
Her letter shows that she wants Karim to become a full mechanic. This goal fits her values of craft, learning and kindness.
A year is too long to plan, so Ines divides her goal into weekly steps. Each week Karim will learn one new skill, from tyres to gears.
Ines sees that some tasks shout for attention, while others matter more but stay silent. The noisy tasks are not always the important ones.
Ines decides to protect Friday mornings for the work that matters most. She turns off her phone, and puts a sign on the door.
Every Sunday Ines spends twenty minutes looking at the week that has passed and the week ahead. She asks what went well, what should change and what matters most.
A man asks Ines to repair a dozen bicycles in two days. She says no, because to say yes would mean doing poor work and letting Karim down.
There are 168 hours in every week, and nobody receives more than that. Ines sees that how she spends them is a choice, whether she makes it deliberately or not.
Ines discovers that she is short-tempered and careless whenever she is tired. Sleep, she decides, is not a luxury but part of the plan.
Ines decides that her prices must be fair to the customer and to her shop. She writes them on a board outside, so that everyone can see them.
Karim breaks a customer's wheel while he is learning to fix it. He is afraid to tell Ines, and he hides it behind the bench.
Ines tells Karim that the mistake is understandable, but that hiding it was not right. Together they phone the customer and replace the wheel.
A good mechanic asks what is wrong before she picks up a tool. Ines realises that people deserve the same care, because advice without understanding often misses the point.
Mr Weiss is angry about the cost of repairing an old bicycle. When Ines asks him why, she learns that it belonged to his late wife.
Ines offers to do the most important repairs first and the rest later. Mr Weiss can afford it, and her work will be paid for fairly.
A buyer offers a large order at a price that would cost Ines money on every bicycle. She cannot find a fair deal, so she politely says no.
Ines is strongest at hard repairs, while Karim is wonderful with nervous customers. When they share the work according to their strengths, the whole shop runs better.
Every Friday Ines and Karim hold a short meeting about the week. They also paint their shared values on the wall, so that nobody has to be told what to do.
Ines must tell Karim that his latest repair is not safe, and she does not want to hurt him. She decides that honesty and kindness can work together if she is careful.
Her sister Lucia asks Ines for a loan, and the shop cannot afford much. Ines feels pulled between her family and her business.
Ines is honest with her sister about what the shop can afford. They agree on a smaller amount and a clear plan for paying it back.
A manager from Velo World comes to the shop and offers to buy it. The money is good, and Ines is tempted for the first time in years.
Ines holds the offer up against each of her five values in turn. Some of them say yes, and some say no, so the answer is not simple.
In the end Ines declines the offer, because her work is what gives her days their meaning. She does not think that other people are wrong to accept such offers.
In a stressful month Ines loses her temper with a rude customer, and she says things that she does not mean. Afterwards she feels ashamed and a long way from her values.
Ines remembers that a compass can be thrown off by a lump of iron close by. She decides that she has only drifted, and that she can correct her course.
Ines joins a monthly repair day at the local hall, where she shows children how to mend their bicycles. Teaching them gives her more joy than almost anything else.
Ines sees that a good life needs care in four areas, which are body, mind, people and purpose. If one is ignored, the others begin to suffer.
Ines decides to learn how to repair electric bicycles, because the future of her trade is changing. Learning is one of her values, so she studies a little every evening.
A year after she started, Ines reads her letter from the future again. Much of what she wrote has already come true, in smaller ways than she expected.
Karim passes his final test and becomes a full mechanic at Second Wheel. Ines tells him about the compass and asks him to write his own five words.
Living by your principles is not about perfect rules or perfect days. It means choosing your direction, checking it often, and correcting your course with kindness whenever you drift.
C1C2: From the moment she turned the sign on Second Wheel each morning, Ines was swept along by a stream of punctures, broken chains and impatient customers. She was good at her work and proud of it, yet she had the uneasy sense of reacting to everything and steering nothing. It felt like pedalling very hard down a road without knowing where it went.

Above the workbench hung her grandfather's brass compass, a small heavy thing that had crossed oceans in his coat pocket before it came to rest on her wall. One quiet evening Ines found herself staring at it and realised that it measured direction, never speed, and that she had spent years thinking only about the second. Pace is of little use, she thought, if the heading is wrong, and hers had never once been checked.

Busyness, Ines saw, can be a clever disguise for drifting, because a full diary gives the pleasant illusion that every hour is well spent. She pulled a notepad toward her and asked herself a question she had avoided for years, which was what she wanted her work and her life to stand for. The page stayed blank for a long time before the first honest word finally appeared, and then others followed.

She began by listing everything that seemed important, from success and comfort to loyalty, humour and fairness, until the page held twenty words in untidy handwriting. A value, she decided, is a quality you would keep choosing even when nobody was watching and nothing was gained by it, which is quite different from something that merely sounds admirable. Some of the words survived that test with ease, while others, to her surprise, quietly faded from the page.

The hardest part was the cutting, since every word on the list had a claim on her and none of them was foolish. She forced herself to ask which she would protect first on a difficult day, when money was short and everyone wanted something, and the answers were more revealing than she had expected. By the time the shop closed that evening, only five words remained, and they looked small, plain and strong.

Honesty, craft, family, learning and kindness: Ines wrote the five words in large letters on a card and pinned it beside her grandfather's compass, where she would see it every day. They were not a slogan for customers or a promise to anyone else, but a private description of the person she wanted to be. Looking at them, she felt oddly calmer, like a traveller who has finally found the north.

She drew a small flag on a hill to stand for a goal and an arrow pointing off the page to stand for a value, and she saw that they play different roles. You can reach a goal and cross it off, but you can never finish being honest or kind, since those are directions in which you keep travelling. Goals matter a great deal, but they are best chosen only after the heading has been properly decided.

When she traced her five words back to their source, Ines found her grandfather standing behind nearly all of them, bent over an engine and refusing to let a job leave his hands half done. Many of our values arrive through family, culture and experience before we are old enough to question them, and there is nothing shameful in that. The real step is to examine them honestly and decide, as an adult, which ones to keep.

When a customer bellowed that his repair was a day late, Ines felt her anger flare up like a match, and the old reflex to shout back was ready. Then she noticed the narrow gap between what had happened and what she was about to do, and she understood that her freedom lives inside that gap. She apologised for the delay in an even voice, and the man's anger had nowhere to go.

Ines caught herself saying that she had to open early, had to answer every message and had to accept every job, as though she were a puppet on strings. She tried replacing those words with I choose to, which obliged her to ask whether the choice was still the right one, and sometimes it was not. The small change of phrase did not alter her tasks, but it returned the pen to her own hand.

She could not control the weather, which ruled the number of customers, or the price of parts, or the opinions people posted about her on the internet. What she could control was the quality of her repairs, the manner of her words and the next small step she took, and she resolved to spend her energy there. It is remarkable how much worry evaporates when you sort a problem into those two piles.

One grey Monday a large chain called Velo World opened its doors two streets away, with bright lights, rows of shining bicycles and prices that Ines could never match. She spent a sleepless night picturing her empty shop, and then, at breakfast, she put the problem through her sorting exercise and found that most of it belonged in the pile of things beyond her power. What remained within her power turned out to be surprisingly useful, and it could be started that very morning.

A friend suggested that Ines hint to customers that the large shop used careless mechanics, but she shook her head, because it was neither proven nor true. Her principles told her to compete by excellence, by speed where she could manage it and by honest explanations of every repair, and to say nothing untrue about anyone. A victory won through a lie, she reasoned, would cost her more than the defeat she feared.

A new customer brought in his bicycle for a brake repair, and when Ines examined it she saw that the old pads still had months of life left in them. He would have paid for new ones without a second thought, and she was behind on her bills, so the temptation was real and quite specific. Principles are rarely tested by great dramas; they are tested at small workbenches by quiet opportunities like this.

Ines laid the old pad in the customer's palm, showed him how much material remained, and told him that he did not need a replacement for some months. She lost a small sale that day, but he thanked her warmly, and a month later he returned with his wife and two neighbours who all needed bicycles repaired. Honesty seldom pays at the moment it is practised, though it tends to pay handsomely over time.

Integrity, Ines decided, is simply the state of being whole, in which what you say, what you believe and what you do all point the same way. Each time she acted against her values, however slightly, she suspected that a small voice inside her lost a little faith in her, and that this lost trust was hard to rebuild. When her actions matched her words, she felt a quiet strength that no compliment from a customer could give.

Ines made herself a small promise, a ten-minute walk before the shop opened, and she kept it through rain and darkness and a morning when she would much rather have stayed in bed. It seemed trivial, yet every fulfilled promise acted like a small deposit in an account of self-respect, and the balance grew steadily. She noticed, with some surprise, that she was beginning to believe her own intentions again.

To make the habit stick, Ines kept it deliberately tiny, one sentence in a notebook, and tied it to something she already did every day, which was making her morning tea. She left the notebook beside the kettle where it was impossible to overlook, and the old habit pulled the new one along behind it like a trailer. Ambitious plans fail, she observed, far more often than modest ones that actually happen.

One Sunday Ines wrote a letter from the person she hoped to be in five years, describing in detail an ordinary good Tuesday in the shop, the people in it and how she felt as she locked the door. She was surprised that the picture contained very little luxury and a great deal of calm, trust and skill. To begin with a clear picture of where you are heading, she realised, makes every present choice easier to judge.

Among the details of her letter was the image of Karim, her young helper, working confidently at the bench with a customer's wheel in his hands. It was a goal that flowed directly from three of her values, craft, learning and kindness, and so she adopted it as her main aim for the coming year. A goal that grows from a principle, she found, carries a kind of energy that an arbitrary target never does.

A year is far too large a unit to plan around, so Ines cut her goal into weekly pieces, each one small enough to attempt without dread. In the first week Karim would learn to mend a puncture properly, in the second he would study gears, and in the third he would set up a wheel that ran true. A mountain, she thought, is climbed by people who simply keep taking the next step.

Her phone buzzed, the shop bell rang and a delivery arrived, yet the task that mattered most that morning, teaching Karim to build a wheel, made no sound at all. Ines grasped that some tasks shout and others merely matter, and that if she answered only the loudest ones, her most important work would never begin. It was a plain observation, but she wished that she had made it ten years earlier.

To defend her important work against the clamour, Ines set aside Friday mornings as a protected time for teaching Karim and planning the weeks ahead. She switched off her phone and hung a small sign on the door, and she discovered that the world rarely collapsed while she was away from it for three hours. Time for what matters, she concluded, is never simply found lying about, but must be deliberately made.

Her Sunday review took only twenty minutes, in which she looked back at the past week and asked what had gone well, what she regretted and what she would change. Then she looked at the coming week and chose three things that truly mattered, and only afterwards did she fit in everything else. This small ritual worked like the daily glance at a compass, nudging her back to her heading before she had wandered far.

When a neighbour asked her to repair a dozen bicycles within two days, Ines felt the old reflex to agree and to prove that she could never be beaten by a challenge. She declined, politely and clearly, because accepting would have meant rushed work and an empty Friday morning, and both of those would have betrayed her principles. Every no, she realised, is simply the protection of some more important yes that she has already given.

A week contains exactly 168 hours, and the rich and the poor, the busy and the idle all receive precisely the same number. Ines considered how many of those hours she had spent without deciding anything, simply drifting from one demand to the next, and the thought was sobering. Time cannot be saved or stretched, only spent, and she preferred to spend it on purpose.

After a week of late nights, Ines lost her temper with Karim over a trivial mistake, and the moment she heard her own voice she knew that exhaustion had been speaking. Tired people tend to choose worse, to see problems in a darker light and to forget their principles at the very moment they need them. She began to treat sleep as part of her plan rather than a reward for finishing it.

Money is where principles often become uncomfortable, and Ines wrestled with prices that had to be fair to her customers while remaining high enough to keep the shop alive. She settled on a simple standard, charging what she would consider reasonable if she were on the other side of the counter, and she posted the prices on a board where anyone could read them. Fairness hidden in secrecy, she thought, is not really fairness at all, but only a private opinion.

In his second month of training, Karim bent a customer's wheel so badly that it was beyond saving, and for an hour he hid it behind a stack of tyres, sick with fear. When Ines found it, her first instinct was to be angry, but she remembered that one of her values was learning and that learning without mistakes is not learning at all. She sat down on an upturned crate beside him and asked him, quite calmly, what had gone wrong.

She told Karim that the mistake itself was forgivable and that the hiding of it was the real problem, and she wanted him to understand both parts of that sentence. Together they telephoned the customer, explained what had happened and ordered a new wheel, which Karim paid for out of his own small wages with a little help from the shop. It was kind and it was honest, and Ines was relieved to find that those two can sit together.

Any competent mechanic knows that you diagnose a fault before you repair it, for otherwise you merely change parts and hope. Ines saw that exactly the same rule applies to conversations, in which advice offered before real understanding tends to answer the wrong question and to make the other person feel dismissed. So she made a habit of asking, and then asking again, until she was certain she had understood.

Mr Weiss, an elderly customer, complained fiercely about the cost of repairing a very ordinary old bicycle, and Ines might have dismissed him as a miser. Because she asked him questions first, she discovered that the bicycle had belonged to his wife, who had died the previous winter, and that he could not bear to see it rust. The anger on the surface was only a thin cover for grief, and the true problem was one that she could actually help with.

Rather than fighting over the price, Ines searched for an arrangement in which both of them would gain, and she proposed doing the essential repairs at once and the cosmetic ones over the following months. Mr Weiss could afford that, the bicycle would be safe to ride, and Ines would be paid fairly for every hour of her work. The best agreements, she noticed, leave both people feeling that they have won something, rather than one person feeling that the other has taken it.

Not every negotiation could be turned into a happy ending, and a man who wanted twenty repairs at a price below her costs showed no interest in a fairer figure. Ines thanked him and declined, accepting that a bad deal made out of fear would harm her shop and her self-respect for much longer than a lost order. The willingness to walk away, she saw, is part of what makes honest bargaining possible.

It gradually became clear that Ines excelled at complicated repairs, whereas Karim possessed a gift for putting anxious customers at their ease with a joke and a cup of tea. Instead of insisting that he become a copy of her, she arranged the work so that each of them did what they did best, and the shop hummed with a new smoothness. Differences, handled well, are not obstacles to a good team but extra tools in the box.

Every Friday the two of them held a short meeting in which they reviewed the week, discussed difficult customers and decided what to improve next. Ines also added Karim's thoughts to the card of values on the wall, so that when a decision arose, neither of them needed a long set of rules, only a clear sense of what mattered. People who share principles can be trusted to make good choices without being watched.

Karim's latest brake repair was not safe, and Ines faced a miniature crisis between two of her values, since honesty demanded that she speak and kindness urged her to spare him. She resolved to do both, naming the fault clearly and at once, but describing it as a skill still to be learned rather than a failure of his character. He nodded, slightly red in the face, and asked, to her great relief, whether he could have another go.

Her sister Lucia, who was struggling with a sudden bill, asked whether she might borrow a sum that would leave Second Wheel dangerously short for the winter. Family was one of Ines's five values, yet so was the shop that fed them both, and for a day she felt torn exactly in half. She did not decide at once, for she knew that important choices made under pressure are often poorly made.

Ines explained the true state of her finances with a frankness that surprised them both, and together with Lucia she worked out a smaller loan that the shop could survive. They wrote down how it would be repaid, not because they distrusted one another but because clarity protects a relationship better than good intentions. Lucia hugged her afterwards and said that she felt more respected than if Ines had simply handed her the money.

In late spring a smartly dressed manager from Velo World walked into Second Wheel with a generous offer to buy the shop, the name and the customers. The sum would have cleared Ines's debts and given her a comfortable year, and for the first time in a long while she felt a real pull toward giving up the daily struggle. She asked for a week to think about it, and she meant every minute of that week to be used.

She went through the offer word by word, asking what honesty, craft, family, learning and kindness would each advise, and she discovered that the answers did not agree. Family and ease said accept, while craft and learning said that she would be selling the very work that gave her days their meaning. A set of principles does not make decisions for you, she saw, but it does ask better questions than panic can.

After a week of careful thought, Ines thanked the manager for his generosity and declined, because the shop was the place where her craft and her teaching actually lived. She did not believe that people who made a different choice were weak or wrong, for their principles and circumstances might point elsewhere, and she said as much to Lucia. Living by your principles means holding yourself to them, not holding everyone else to them.

During a wretched, rainy month in which nothing seemed to go well, Ines snapped at a rude customer and said several things that she bitterly regretted before the bell had stopped ringing. She felt ashamed and far from the person she had written about in her letter, and a cruel little voice told her that all her principles had been a pretence. It was a harsh judgement, and it was also a mistaken one, as she would soon begin to see.

Her grandfather had taught her that a compass needle can be dragged off its true heading by iron or a magnet close at hand, and that the sensible response is to move away and check again. Ines took the same view of her bad month, deciding that she had been pulled off course by pressure and tiredness, and that one failure did not cancel her direction. She apologised to the customer the next morning, and she felt her heading return.

Surrounding yourself with people who share your direction helps you to keep it, so Ines joined a group of volunteers who ran a monthly bicycle repair day at the community hall. Children arrived with bent wheels and flat tyres, left with their bicycles working, and several of them stayed on to ask how the brakes really worked. She went home tired, happy and entirely sure that she was spending her hours in the right way.

Ines drew four circles on a sheet of paper and labelled them body, mind, people and purpose, and then she honestly rated how much attention she had given to each. She had neglected her body, which she had treated as a tool, and her friendships, which she had sacrificed to the shop, and the imbalance explained a good deal of her tiredness. Like a bicycle, a person runs best when every part is looked after, and not only the one that squeaks.

Electric bicycles were becoming common, and Ines saw that a craftsperson who stopped learning would soon be left behind, so she began to study their motors and batteries in the evenings. It was awkward to be a beginner again after so many years of confident skill, yet the discomfort reminded her what Karim must feel every day. Growth, she found, always begins with the willingness to be bad at something for a while.

On a cold March morning, a year to the day since she had first stared at the compass, Ines took out her letter and read it slowly. Much of what it described had quietly come true, not through a dramatic transformation but through hundreds of small decisions made in line with five plain words. She laughed at the parts that were still unfinished and added a few lines to describe the year ahead.

Within the year Karim could dismantle, rebuild and true a wheel faster than his teacher, and he passed his final assessment with only a few nervous glances at Ines. She presented him with a plain card, told him the story of the compass and asked him to write down his own five values, which he did over a long and thoughtful evening. His list was different from hers, and she thought that this was exactly as it should be.

Ines locked the shop at sunset and glanced at her grandfather's compass, and she understood that a principled life is not a matter of flawless behaviour or rigid rules. It is a matter of choosing a direction, checking it regularly, and returning to it patiently and without self-contempt each time the world pulls you aside. The road will always be uneven, but with a clear heading, it is yours.
